newsitem.title: JAPAN: Deng's death not seen affecting Japan investment.
newsitem.headline: Deng's death not seen affecting Japan investment.

text.p: The death of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping is not likely to affect Japanese financial investment in China as the political situation there is expected to remain stable, underwriters said on Thursday.
They said Japanese investors were not expected to worry that China's sovereign credit rating may be lowered due to his death.

"Investors may be slightly cautious but we're not likely to see them actually sell samurai bonds issued by Chinese firms, particularly after Moody's announcement," said Hisao Hosoya, a manager of the corporate research department at Kokusai Securities.
Moody's Investors Service said on Wednesday that Deng's death should not affect the direction of China's economic policy and will have no impact on its A3 sovereign rating.
Moody's said it had already factored in the possible death of Deng in its assessment of China's credit rating.
"Deng's death is not expected to have a major impact on international financial markets," Hosoya said.
Japanese investors are expected to stay calm as they believe that there will not be major changes in the political situation in China under Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin, the underwriters said.

"If Deng had died 10 years ago then Japanese investors might have pulled out their investment quickly, but it's not like that now. The political situation appears stable," said a senior underwriter at one of Japan's "Big Four" securities houses.
"I think China already knows that political uncertainty or turmoil would result in the immediate withdrawal of foreign investment," the underwriter said.
Kokusai's Hosoya said that he is not expecting to see a major change in global money flows.

"I don't expect to see much change in the flow of money," he said. "Also, U.S. investors are not expected to move funds out of China as (U.S. President Bill) Clinton's comments mainly stated Deng's accomplishments and did not mention investments."
